title: Navigating uncertain waters: a critical review of inferring foraging behaviour from location and dive data in pinnipeds

subsections.subsection_title: Foundations of Diving and Foraging Ecology
subsections.content:
Diving and foraging ecology in pinnipeds is grounded in the interaction between physiological constraint and prey acquisition. Breath-hold foraging is limited by oxygen storage, aerobic dive capacity, and the mechanical consequences of pressure at depth; in deep-diving mammals, enlarged blood and muscle oxygen stores and early lung collapse shape the duration, depth, and structure of routine foraging dives ref [1]. These constraints mean that dive profiles are not simply behavioural choices, but emergent outcomes of trade-offs among transit costs, bottom access time, prey encounter opportunities, and recovery requirements.

At the same time, foraging is not equivalent to diving per se. Direct observations and stomach-temperature records show that feeding can occur soon after departure, across multiple dive types, and with substantial individual variability in rate and location, underscoring the patchy and probabilistic nature of prey capture in marine systems ref [2], ref [3]. Studies integrating movement, habitat, and prey-ingestion proxies further show that successful foraging reflects the coupling of horizontal search, vertical habitat use, and bottom-phase investment rather than any single dive metric alone ref [4].

This conceptual distinction is crucial for pinniped survey work because many commonly used proxies capture foraging effort better than foraging success. Validation studies in elephant seals and fur seals demonstrate that bottom duration, ascent or descent rates, and other dive characteristics can predict prey capture attempts with moderate to good accuracy, but that model performance is scale dependent and species specific ref [5], ref [6]. Thus, the ecological foundation for behavioural inference is one of constrained optimization under uncertainty: dive behaviour contains information about prey exploitation, but only imperfectly and always through the filter of physiology, habitat, and prey behaviour ref [1], ref [4], ref [5].

subsections.subsection_title: Biologging and Telemetry as a Conceptual Lens
subsections.content:
Biologging and telemetry provide the conceptual and methodological bridge between unobservable underwater behaviour and ecological inference in pinnipeds. More than a set of tools, they constitute an observational lens that converts animal movement, diving, posture, and local environmental context into interpretable behavioural proxies across scales ranging from individual dives to basin-scale migrations. Reviews of aquatic telemetry and marine megavertebrate satellite tracking emphasize how these technologies transformed marine ecology from largely descriptive natural history into a quantitatively explicit, hypothesis-driven science capable of resolving where, when, and under what conditions animals use the ocean [2], ref [9].

This lens has broadened substantially with advances in miniaturization, sensor integration, and analytical workflows. Contemporary biologging combines location data with time-depth recorders, accelerometers, magnetometers, cameras, and sometimes physiological or environmental sensors, allowing researchers to examine the coupling among movement, energetics, prey encounters, and habitat structure rather than treating space use alone as the endpoint [4], ref [5]. For air-breathing divers such as pinnipeds, this multimodal perspective is especially important because dives are discrete behavioural units embedded within larger movement trajectories, and each sensor type captures only a partial manifestation of the underlying foraging process.

At the same time, telemetry is not a transparent window onto behaviour. Inference depends on device error, sampling resolution, tag effects, transmission constraints, and the assumptions used to map observed patterns onto latent states such as transit, search, or prey capture [2], ref [9], ref [10]. Accordingly, biologging is best framed as a conceptual lens that is powerful but selective: it expands access to otherwise hidden behaviours while requiring careful validation and critical interpretation before location and dive records are equated with foraging success or ecological function [4], ref [5].

subsections.subsection_title: Inferring Behaviour from Animal-Borne Sensors
subsections.content:
A central challenge in pinniped biologging is that behaviour is latent, whereas sensors record only partial mechanical proxies such as depth, acceleration, or position. Behavioural inference therefore depends on explicit translation models that map sensor signatures onto ecologically meaningful states, ideally with quantified uncertainty. At the fine scale, accelerometers have been used to detect prey-capture-related head or body movements, but validation studies show that these signals are imperfect proxies rather than direct observations of ingestion ref [11], ref [12].

Validation against animal-borne video has been especially important in demonstrating both the promise and the limits of sensor-based inference. In Australian fur seals, head-mounted accelerometers detected many attempted prey captures, yet could not reliably distinguish prey type, successful versus unsuccessful capture, or all non-feeding head movements, highlighting substantial false-positive structure and the need for correction factors ref [11]. Comparable work in penguins showed that supervised machine-learning classifiers trained on video-labelled accelerometry can recover prey-handling events with relatively strong performance, illustrating how ground-truthed models can move beyond heuristic thresholds toward reproducible behavioural annotation ref [12].

At broader temporal scales, hidden-state approaches provide a conceptual bridge between movement metrics and unobserved behavioural modes. Hidden Markov models are particularly valuable because they treat behaviour as a latent stochastic process, accommodate serial dependence, and allow transition probabilities to vary with environmental covariates ref [5]. For pinnipeds, this logic underpins classification of tracks or dive sequences into putative resident, transit, or foraging phases, but it also underscores a key caution: inferred states are model-dependent abstractions whose ecological meaning is strongest when supported by independent validation, preferably from complementary sensors or direct observations ref [11], ref [5].

subsections.subsection_title: Conservation Relevance of Movement and Behavioural Ecology
subsections.content:
Movement and behavioural ecology are central to conservation because population decline in the ocean is rarely random in space or time. Marine defaunation has restructured food webs, compressed ranges, and reduced the functional roles of marine predators, making it essential to identify where pinnipeds forage, rest, and move in relation to risk [1]. More broadly, climate change is shifting prey fields, phenology, and habitat suitability for marine vertebrates, so behaviourally explicit movement data are increasingly necessary to distinguish transient redistribution from loss of critical foraging habitat [3].

For wide-ranging predators, conservation effectiveness depends on matching management scales to ecological scales. Movement ecology has therefore become a practical bridge between observation and intervention, informing dynamic fisheries measures, bycatch mitigation, and the design of protected-area networks that account for mobile top predators rather than static habitat alone [6]. This is particularly important because many marine protected areas remain smaller than the routine movement domains of top consumers, requiring networked and adaptive approaches instead of isolated reserves [4].

Marine mammals also have special conservation value as sentinels: their distribution, body condition, contaminant burdens, and disease dynamics integrate environmental change across trophic levels and over long time scales [7]. As a result, behavioural shifts inferred from telemetry can support ecological risk assessment and early warning of ocean change, including contaminant exposure, emerging disease, and climate-driven ecosystem disruption [8,9]. In pinnipeds, robust inference about foraging behaviour is therefore not only an ecological question, but a conservation tool for anticipating ecosystem change and prioritizing management action.

subsections.subsection_title: Human Interactions and Observational Applications
subsections.content:
Animal-borne sensors are increasingly used not only to infer foraging states, but also to observe how marine predators interact with human activities in situ. In seabirds, bird-borne cameras paired with GPS have shown that apparent area-restricted search can occur both around fishing vessels and during non-fishery foraging, demonstrating that movement patterns alone may overestimate direct fishery dependence or interaction rates ref [21]. More broadly, combining tracking with vessel information has transformed the study of overlap between predators and fisheries, but also highlights that spatial co-occurrence is not equivalent to behavioural interaction.

This distinction is especially relevant for pinnipeds, where location and dive data are often interpreted as feeding proxies in landscapes heavily modified by fishing, shipping, tourism, aquaculture, and coastal development. Integrating telemetry with ancillary observations, such as animal-borne video, accelerometry, acoustic records, or vessel monitoring system data, can reveal attraction to vessels, depredation on gear, bycatch risk, and behavioural shifts near anthropogenic structures that would remain ambiguous in dive profiles alone ref [2], ref [3], ref [4]. Such observational applications are valuable because they expose the mechanisms behind apparent foraging hotspots and help separate prey-driven responses from human-mediated subsidies or disturbances ref [5], ref [6].

For conservation and management, these approaches support more realistic interpretation of inferred behaviour and can inform mitigation of bycatch, depredation conflicts, and illegal or poorly monitored fishing activity. They also broaden the role of biologging from behavioural inference to evidence generation for ecosystem-based management, especially when used to identify sex-, age-, or colony-specific exposure to anthropogenic risk ref [21], ref [4], ref [7]. In the pinniped context, the central message is methodological as much as ecological: observational validation is often essential when 'foraging behaviour' may actually reflect interaction with people, infrastructure, or fisheries.

subsections.subsection_title: Biologging Platforms and Sensor Modalities
subsections.content:
Biologging platforms used in pinniped studies have evolved from early Argos platform transmitter terminals to highly integrated archival and relay systems that combine movement, dive, and environmental sensing. Early satellite applications on grey and harbor seals showed both the promise and the core engineering challenge of pinniped telemetry: animals surface only briefly, so tag architecture, antenna placement, and transmission logic strongly determine data yield ref [22], ref [23]. In particular, head-mounted or otherwise exposure-optimized antennas, wet/dry or submergence switches, and duty-cycled transmissions substantially improved the number of usable at-sea locations relative to dorsally mounted transmitters alone ref [22], ref [23].

A major transition was the development of Satellite Relay Data Loggers and CTD-SRDLs, which reframed seals not only as tracked predators but also as autonomous oceanographic samplers. These platforms integrated pressure, temperature, conductivity and wet/dry sensors with on-board microcontrollers that abstract dives and hydrographic profiles before Argos relay, allowing biologically and physically informative data return despite severe bandwidth and battery constraints ref [24], ref [25], ref [26]. The generalized CTD-SRDL protocol further formalized this design philosophy: behavioral state classification, broken-stick compression of dive and profile shapes, selective buffering, and transmission scheduling are all embedded in the device, making sensor modality inseparable from onboard analytical design ref [24].

Platform choice therefore reflects study objectives and spatiotemporal context. Archival time-depth-temperature recorders can return high-resolution profiles when recapture is feasible, whereas satellite relay tags trade resolution for coverage and persistence; in some coastal settings, GSM-based phone tags offer a lower-cost alternative for haul-out and resighting data when animals regularly enter network range ref [25], ref [27], ref [28]. Across modalities, the critical point for inference is that each sensor package measures not simply location or diving, but a platform-specific, compressed representation of behavior filtered through attachment geometry, transmission opportunities, and embedded software rules ref [23], ref [24], ref [27].

subsections.subsection_title: Location Error, Filtering, and Data Recovery
subsections.content:
Location error is a central constraint when inferring foraging from pinniped telemetry because behavioural metrics such as path tortuosity, residence, and habitat association are highly sensitive to Argos uncertainty. Validation against Fastloc GPS showed that Argos errors on free-ranging pinnipeds are larger and more skewed than nominal CLS specifications, with low-quality classes (0, A, B) dominating many deployments and displaying pronounced longitudinal structure and heavy tails ref [29]. Captive gray seal trials similarly demonstrated anisotropic errors and showed that LC A can be comparable to LC 1, whereas LC B remains substantially less precise; simple speed filtering chiefly removes extreme outliers rather than fully resolving observation error ref [33].

These error structures motivate explicit filtering and state-space reconstruction rather than naive use of raw tracks. GPS-based evaluations indicate that speed filtering combined with Kalman or Bayesian state-space models can substantially improve track realism, but performance depends on the chosen speed threshold, the underlying error model, and transmission density ref [30], ref [32]. Analyses relative to Fastloc GPS further suggest that Argos-CLS Kalman-filtered locations are generally improved over legacy least-squares solutions, especially for low-quality classes, and can yield state-space reconstructions with kilometre-scale rather than tens-of-kilometres uncertainty under favourable conditions ref [31]. Nonetheless, model sensitivity to preprocessing and species-specific surfacing behaviour means that error distributions should be tailored to study system and tag platform wherever possible ref [29], ref [32].

Data recovery imposes an additional design constraint because biologgers often collect far more information than can be transmitted. Study yield depends jointly on tag retention, satellite coverage, bandwidth, and duty cycling, so deployment design should optimize expected recovery rather than tag count alone ref [34]. In practice, incomplete transmission and the abstraction of dive and location records require analysts to align behavioural questions with the temporal resolution actually recoverable, and to treat filtering, interpolation, and missingness as part of the inferential framework rather than as purely technical preprocessing steps ref [30], ref [34].

subsections.subsection_title: Dive Data Abstraction and Analytical Design
subsections.content:
Dive records are already abstractions of three-dimensional underwater behaviour, and further simplification is often unavoidable when storage, battery life, bandwidth, or tag recovery limit what can be retained or transmitted. This makes analytical design inseparable from data abstraction: choices about sampling interval, onboard processing, and which dive attributes are preserved determine which behavioural questions can later be asked objectively [1], [3]. Early work emphasized that abstraction should minimize subjective shape classification by deriving automated, comparable descriptors from time–depth profiles, including inflection-point representations and scalar indices such as time allocation at depth [1].

A major development in pinniped telemetry has been the use of broken-stick models to summarize dives as a small number of vertices, as implemented widely in CTD-SRDLs [2]. This approach efficiently captures gross dive geometry, but only a small fraction of original samples is retained, so inference depends on whether biologically relevant structure survives compression [2]. Photopoulou et al. showed that abstracted profiles can be supplemented with post hoc uncertainty metrics, including dive-zone indices that quantify goodness-of-fit and reveal systematic variation in abstraction error among dive types [2]. This is important because square, drift, and highly sinuous dives may be represented with unequal fidelity, potentially biasing behavioural classification if compression error is ignored [2].

Analytical design should therefore begin before deployment. Tag programming governs not only temporal resolution, but the continuity and regularity of behavioural time series, both of which are critical for state-space and hidden Markov analyses [3]. Simulation studies show that frequent, regular observations can sometimes compensate for lower spatial precision, whereas long programmed gaps can obscure short-lived behavioural transitions even with accurate locations [3]. For pinniped studies that combine location and dive data, the central design problem is thus not simply maximizing data volume, but matching abstraction and transmission rules to the temporal scale of the behaviours of interest, while preserving uncertainty information needed for robust inference [1], [2], [3].

subsections.subsection_title: Field Deployment, Tag Effects, and Animal Welfare
subsections.content:
Field deployment choices in pinniped studies are inseparable from questions of inference quality and animal welfare. Capture, restraint, handling, and attachment can alter subsequent behaviour, particularly during the first post-release period, while attachment method, tag position, and package geometry can impose hydrodynamic and thermal costs that bias estimates of natural foraging effort [1], [2]. Consequently, deployment protocols should be treated as part of study design rather than a purely logistical step.

Evidence from pinnipeds suggests that handling effects and instrument effects are not equivalent. In lactating Antarctic fur seals, the first trip after capture and instrumentation was broadly representative of the second, implying that short deployments need not necessarily induce strong acute behavioural artefacts; however, bulkier packages increased time at sea and reduced pup growth, highlighting sensitivity to instrument size and streamlining [1]. Broader reviews across marine mammals similarly show that externally attached devices can alter swimming, haul-out behaviour, maternal attendance, and trip duration, even where survival effects are not detectable [2]. Experimental work on captive Steller sea lions further supports a mechanistic basis for these biases: added drag, but not buoyancy within a natural range, reduced swim speed, underscoring that frontal area and shape may matter more than tag mass alone [3].

Best practice therefore favors the smallest, most streamlined packages, short attachment durations where possible, and explicit reporting of handling time, attachment materials, analgesia or sedation, and post-deployment monitoring [1], [2]. Welfare review should extend beyond immediate survival to include wound healing, behavioural recovery, offspring consequences, and the possibility that different device generations are not directly comparable [1], [2]. For studies inferring foraging from movement and dive records, unquantified tag effects risk being mistaken for ecological signals.

subsections.subsection_title: Applications of Data Acquisition in Pinniped Ecology
subsections.content:
Beyond methodological concerns, location and dive data have transformed understanding of pinniped ecology by revealing where, when, and under what environmental conditions animals forage. Early telemetry studies showed that grey and harbour seals organize time at sea into distinct behavioural modes, linking square-wave or benthic-associated dives, trip duration, and repeated use of particular feeding areas to likely foraging activity near haul-out sites or along transit routes ref [42], ref [43]. Subsequent multi-sensor deployments extended this perspective from local movements to broad seascape use, showing that southern elephant seals commute over thousands of kilometres to shelf breaks, frontal systems, and other relocatable hydrographic features where dive structure shifts markedly, consistent with changes in prey field and foraging mode ref [9].

These datasets have also enabled biologging to contribute directly to ecosystem oceanography. Instrumented elephant seals have mapped poorly sampled Southern Ocean frontal structure, greatly increased winter hydrographic coverage beneath sea ice, and even allowed inference of sea-ice formation rates from repeated salinity profiles ref [10]. Such applications illustrate that data acquisition in pinnipeds can support both predator ecology and physical oceanography, especially in regions inaccessible to ships and floats.

At population scales, integrated movement-behaviour datasets have been used to estimate complete activity budgets and to test intrinsic and extrinsic drivers of space use. In sympatric grey and harbour seals, combining telemetry-derived movement and behavioural states showed seasonal, sex-specific allocation among hauling out, resting at sea, foraging, and travelling, while also revealing limited temporal segregation between species and substantial use of offshore resting ref [11]. Collectively, these applications underscore that biologging data are most powerful when interpreted as ecological evidence on habitat use, energetic scheduling, and predator-environment coupling rather than as simple proxies for foraging success alone ref [42], ref [43], ref [9], ref [11].

subsections.section_title: Inference from Dive and Movement Data
subsections.subsection_title: Dive Metrics as Proxies for Foraging Effort and Success
subsections.content:
Dive variables have long been used as indirect indicators of pinniped foraging, especially when direct measures of prey capture are unavailable. Common proxies include bottom time, sinuosity or wiggle counts during the bottom phase, dive depth, ascent–descent symmetry, and post-dive recovery, all interpreted as reflecting investment in prey search or exploitation. Methodological work has sought to preserve such behavioural signal even in compressed telemetry records: new indices derived from low-resolution profiles can recover variation in inferred foraging effort from high-resolution dives, while within-dive metrics provide a more explicit quantification of putative search intensity during specific dive phases rather than across whole dives alone ref [46], ref [9].

However, the central question is not whether dive metrics vary, but whether they predict feeding success. Validation studies show that some dive characteristics do correlate with prey capture attempts, but relationships are context dependent and imperfect. In Australian fur seals, dive shape and bottom-phase characteristics predicted foraging success when checked against animal-borne video, supporting the utility of dive-based proxies while also highlighting substantial unexplained variance ref [49]. Similar tests using independent prey-capture data found that dive patterns alone can provide useful but only probabilistic estimates of success, with predictive skill improving when vertical metrics are combined with horizontal movement information ref [48], ref [11]. Measures of horizontal and vertical search intensity in harbour seals likewise suggest that area-restricted movement and within-dive search can index effort, but effort should not be conflated with intake ref [14].

The main limitation is that proxies derived from dives more often capture foraging effort or opportunity than realized energy gain. Direct feeding indicators such as stomach temperature telemetry reveal temporal patterns of ingestion that are not always obvious from dive structure alone ref [12]. Accordingly, dive-based inference is strongest when framed as a hypothesis about relative search effort or prey encounter likelihood and when calibrated with independent sensors, videos, or prey-capture tags. This has motivated a shift from using single summary metrics toward multivariate, validation-based approaches that explicitly distinguish search, capture attempt, and successful ingestion ref [48], ref [49], ref [12].

subsections.section_title: Inference from Dive and Movement Data
subsections.subsection_title: Behavioral Classification and Three-Dimensional Dive-Movement Patterns
subsections.content:
Behavioral classification of pinniped dives has progressed from visual typologies based on depth–time traces to more formal multivariate and shape-based schemes. In Weddell seals, manual, discriminant, cluster, and geometric approaches converged on a small set of recurrent dive forms—square, triangular, skewed, and long-duration rectangular dives—while also showing that classification boundaries depend on the variables emphasized and that within-dive function cannot be inferred unambiguously from profile shape alone ref [53]. Early field studies nevertheless established the enduring logic of such classes: in grey seals, directed transit was associated with repeated V-shaped dives, whereas slower short trips involved square-wave dives interpreted as foraging, illustrating how dive geometry and horizontal movement jointly inform behavioral interpretation ref [51].

Three-dimensional tracking has made these classifications more mechanistic by revealing how seals actually use space within and across dives. Fine-scale acoustic positioning of lactating Weddell seals showed that individuals concentrated activity in a restricted sector, used much of the water column, and generally converged toward, but rarely remained on, the seabed, consistent with focused search on bentho-pelagic prey rather than simple benthic residence ref [54]. Similarly, three-dimensional analyses of ringed seals distinguished exploratory movement from local search by quantifying time spent and revisits within volumetric cells; local search occurred in about one-third of dives and was concentrated mainly in bottom phases, demonstrating that behavioral state can shift within a single dive ref [6].

These studies highlight a key limitation of two-dimensional proxies: horizontal residency and vertically intensive diving do not map onto foraging in a simple one-to-one fashion. A comparative synthesis across four marine predators found that switching into horizontally resident states was often associated with shorter-than-expected dives for a given depth and longer post-dive surface intervals, contradicting simplistic expectations that greater foraging should always entail longer bottom phases or longer dives ref [9]. Together, classification and 3D movement studies suggest that robust inference requires integrating dive shape, horizontal context, and within-dive spatial structure, rather than treating any single dive form as a definitive indicator of prey encounter or search effort ref [53], ref [54], ref [6].

subsections.section_title: Inference from Dive and Movement Data
subsections.subsection_title: Movement Models for Inferring Foraging States and Search Areas
subsections.content:
Movement models are central to translating noisy horizontal tracks into putative foraging states and spatial search areas. Early approaches commonly used area-restricted search metrics such as first-passage time, which identify scales at which animals slow down and increase path tortuosity, thereby flagging candidate feeding patches and enabling habitat analyses at behaviorally relevant radii ref [57]. Related random-walk mixture models formalized trajectories as switches among movement modes, providing an important bridge from descriptive track statistics to explicit inference on transit versus localized search ref [12].

Subsequent state-space models improved inference by jointly accounting for observation error and latent movement processes, a particularly important advance for Argos-derived pinniped tracks. Robust state-space formulations reduced bias from irregular sampling and large location uncertainty, while comparative evaluations against GPS data showed that inferred search areas can differ markedly among methods, emphasizing that apparent biological hotspots may partly reflect model choice and error structure ref [13], ref [56]. At broader scale, synthesis across taxa has shown that state-space approaches are now the dominant framework for extracting behavioral states from telemetry, but also that state definitions and biological interpretation remain heterogeneous ref [61].

Hidden Markov models and related extensions have further expanded this toolbox by allowing flexible state-dependent step-length and turning-angle distributions, covariate effects, and direct links between movement mode and environment ref [9], ref [16]. In pinnipeds, such approaches have revealed sex- and season-specific tactics in grey seals, illustrating how inferred search states can uncover population structure in foraging strategies while still requiring cautious interpretation as search does not necessarily equal prey capture ref [11]. Overall, movement models are most powerful when search-state inference is validated against independent dive, prey-capture, or environmental data rather than treated as a standalone proxy for foraging success.

subsections.section_title: Inference from Dive and Movement Data
subsections.subsection_title: Physiological and Theoretical Constraints on Dive-Based Inference
subsections.content:
Inference from dive profiles is bounded by basic respiratory physiology. Dive duration reflects the interaction of oxygen stores, metabolic rate, cardiovascular control, and pressure-related constraints, rather than foraging motivation alone. Deep-diving birds and mammals concentrate much of their usable oxygen in blood and muscle, exhibit marked myoglobin enhancement, and often limit pulmonary gas exchange through lung collapse at depth; consequently, similar dive shapes can arise from very different internal physiological states and costs ref [1].

These limits complicate the common assumption that longer or deeper dives imply greater foraging effort. The aerobic dive limit provides a useful benchmark, but both measured and calculated ADLs are context dependent, varying with dive type, stroke effort, thermoregulation, and recent dive history ref [1]. Optimality models further show that dive duration should depend not only on oxygen depletion but also on travel time, patch quality, and the opportunity costs of remaining underwater: in patchy prey fields, terminating a dive early can be adaptive even when oxygen stores remain available ref [9], ref [10]. Thus, short dives need not indicate failed foraging, nor long dives efficient exploitation.

State inference is also sensitive to body condition and other non-foraging constraints. In phocids, changes in lipid stores alter buoyancy and hence drift rate, descent/ascent costs, and glide patterns, so shifts in dive behavior may reflect changing condition as much as prey encounter ref [65]. Digestion and thermoregulation add further ambiguity: heat increment of feeding, thermal substitution, and potentially conflicting circulatory demands among diving, digestion, and heat balance can all alter dive scheduling and recovery times independently of prey capture success ref [11]. Together, these physiological and theoretical considerations caution against treating dive metrics as direct, species-invariant proxies for foraging success.

subsections.section_title: Inference from Dive and Movement Data
subsections.subsection_title: Ontogeny, Sex, Season, and Environmental Drivers of Inferred Foraging Behaviour
subsections.content:
Inference from dive and movement data is strongly conditioned by intrinsic heterogeneity among individuals. Ontogenetic effects are especially important because inexperienced juveniles often show wider, less efficient, or exploratory movement patterns than adults, making apparent area-restricted search or atypical dive sequences poor proxies for profitable foraging if age is ignored. Recently weaned southern elephant seal pups, for example, disperse through broad pelagic areas with behaviour consistent with naïve exploration rather than optimized prey search, while longer-term work on a long-lived marine predator shows that foraging strategies develop progressively with age and experience rather than emerging fully formed at independence ref [45], ref [7].

Sex and body size further modulate inferred foraging behaviour through differences in dive capacity, travel costs, and habitat use. In harbour seals, trip duration, range, and other foraging-trip characteristics vary with body size and sex, implying that identical movement metrics may reflect different energetic strategies in different demographic classes ref [67]. Comparable sex-specific and seasonal tactics have also been documented in grey seals, where state-space analyses revealed shifts in inferred behavioural modes across the annual cycle, and broader comparisons of sympatric grey and harbour seals indicate that activity budgets are jointly structured by intrinsic traits and external conditions ref [49], ref [6].

Environmental context is therefore not simply a backdrop but a determinant of how behavioural proxies should be interpreted. In situ oceanographic conditions can alter movement, dive behaviour, and body condition simultaneously, changing the relationship between search effort and actual foraging success ref [69]. Likewise, habitat associations with bathymetry and productivity in southern elephant seals show that the same dive or transit pattern may carry different ecological meaning across oceanographic domains ref [26]. Overall, robust inference requires demographic and seasonal stratification, and ideally explicit inclusion of environmental covariates, before converting dive-movement patterns into statements about foraging effort or success.

subsections.section_title: Study Design, Ecological Context, and Generalization
subsections.subsection_title: Telemetry, Movement Modeling, and Inference Frameworks
subsections.content:
Inference from pinniped location records depends first on telemetry design. Tag type, duty-cycling, sampling interval, and error structure determine what behaviours can plausibly be inferred, and reviews of marine mammal biologging show strong taxonomic and demographic biases alongside rapid shifts from Argos and TDRs toward multi-sensor GPS platforms ref [72]. Because relocation data are irregular, error-prone, and behaviourally heterogeneous, movement analysis should separate observation from process rather than treating tracks as direct behavioural evidence ref [70], ref [71], ref [73].

This has motivated a progression from descriptive metrics toward process-based movement models. Mixtures of random walks provided an early framework for partitioning tracks into latent movement modes and estimating switching among them from step lengths and turning angles ref [61]. Hidden Markov models and related state-space approaches then formalized behavioural state estimation while allowing transition probabilities to vary with environmental covariates, making explicit the dependence of inferred states on model assumptions ref [13]. For pinnipeds, such models are valuable because apparent area-restricted search, transit, and resting can emerge from different combinations of horizontal movement error, sampling frequency, and unobserved diving activity.

Continuous-time formulations further improve inference when pinniped tracks are irregularly sampled, avoiding arbitrary interpolation or aggregation and allowing tighter matching to dynamic covariates such as currents, fronts, or haul-out state ref [71]. Yet movement states should not be conflated with foraging success: habitat-preference and space-use models estimate relative use, not prey capture, and predictions remain sensitive to accessibility assumptions, autocorrelation, and individual random effects ref [73], ref [70]. Consequently, robust inference frameworks for pinnipeds should integrate telemetry error models, latent behavioural structure, and explicit ecological hypotheses, while treating behavioural labels as probabilistic rather than definitive proxies for foraging.

subsections.section_title: Study Design, Ecological Context, and Generalization
subsections.subsection_title: Oceanographic Context and Environmentally Driven Behavior
subsections.content:
Inference from pinniped movement and diving data is strengthened when behavior is embedded in the oceanographic setting actually experienced by the animal. Fine-scale currents can distort tracks, alter apparent sinuosity, and therefore bias identification of transit versus search behaviour if ignored; current-corrected analyses show that flow fields can fundamentally change behavioral interpretation rather than merely refine it ref [74]. This is especially important in coastal systems where tides, fronts, and bathymetric constrictions structure prey encounter rates over hours to days.

Studies of pinnipeds illustrate that environmentally driven behaviour is often organized around predictable physical features. Harbour seals can concentrate activity at narrow channels and modulate channel use with flood versus ebb tides, consistent with currents shaping prey aggregation or capture efficiency ref [6]. At broader Southern Ocean scales, successful foraging by southern elephant seals has been linked to frontal systems and shelf environments, with gains in condition occurring near the Polar Front and Antarctic shelf waters, and with behaviour varying with in situ hydrographic structure ref [68], ref [10].

These examples caution against treating location or dive metrics as context-free proxies for foraging. Dive depths, benthic versus pelagic use, and inferred prey choice vary with local habitat structure, including sediment, bathymetry, and water depth ref [11]. More generally, coupled animal–environment records show that the same nominal movement state may reflect different ecological processes under different flow regimes or hydrographic domains. Robust inference therefore requires integrating currents, fronts, bathymetry, and water-mass properties into behavioral interpretation, rather than appending them post hoc ref [68], ref [74], ref [6], ref [10].

subsections.section_title: Study Design, Ecological Context, and Generalization
subsections.subsection_title: Intrinsic Drivers, Life History, and Individual Heterogeneity
subsections.content:
Inference from location and dive records is strongly conditioned by intrinsic state. Sex, body size, age, and reproductive strategy can alter trip duration, dive depth, and allocation of time to transit versus subsurface search, such that similar telemetry signatures may reflect different energetic constraints rather than equivalent prey fields. In harbour seals, foraging-trip characteristics vary with body size and sex ref [66], while in grey seals sexual size dimorphism is associated with clear differences in diving behaviour ref [79]. Comparative work on sympatric grey and harbour seals further shows that activity budgets emerge from interacting intrinsic and extrinsic drivers, cautioning against behavior-only interpretations detached from life-history context ref [45].

Ontogeny adds a second major axis of heterogeneity. Juveniles and newly independent animals often exhibit progressive expansion of movement ranges and improving diving capacity, so apparent changes in search intensity may reflect skill acquisition and developing physiological limits rather than shifts in habitat quality. Age-related development of foraging strategies has been documented in long-lived marine predators ref [69], in Galapagos sea lions where age, body mass, and environmental variation jointly shape foraging ontogeny ref [80], in gray seal pups whose diving capability develops under the constraints and benefits of the postweaning fast ref [81], and in Australian sea lions as movements and foraging ranges mature through early life stages ref [11].

Among adults, life-history stage and individual specialization further complicate generalization across populations. State-space analyses of grey seals reveal sex-specific and seasonal foraging tactics ref [60], implying that the same movement model may classify distinct demographic groups differently if intrinsic covariates are omitted. More broadly, study designs that ignore individual heterogeneity risk conflating persistent between-individual tactics with environmentally driven plasticity. Robust inference therefore requires stratification or hierarchical modeling by sex, age, mass, and reproductive status, and explicit caution when extrapolating behavioural proxies from one demographic segment to another.

subsections.section_title: Study Design, Ecological Context, and Generalization
subsections.subsection_title: Biologging for Coupled Animal–Environment Observation
subsections.content:
Biologging has increasingly moved beyond recording animal movement to coupling predator behavior with direct, in situ measurement of the physical environment. In pinnipeds, this shift is especially important because the same dives used to infer foraging can also generate temperature, depth, and in some cases salinity profiles in regions that are otherwise poorly sampled, particularly at high latitudes and along frontal systems ref [25], ref [26]. Instrumented elephant seals demonstrated early on that animal-borne sensors could contribute oceanographically useful thermal profiles at substantial spatial and temporal scale, adding tens of thousands of observations to broader ocean databases while simultaneously contextualizing foraging trips ref [25].

The methodological promise is twofold. First, paired behavioral and hydrographic records reduce reliance on remotely sensed surface proxies when interpreting subsurface foraging decisions. Second, predators can function as adaptive samplers, disproportionately visiting biologically active fronts, shelf breaks, and eddy fields that are often central to prey aggregation ref [26]. Subsequent CTD-SRDL developments extended this framework to near-real-time conductivity–temperature–depth transmission, improving integration with operational observing systems and enabling daily hydrographic profiling to depths approaching 2000 m in some taxa ref [26]. These platforms have revealed frontal structure, seasonal upper-ocean variability, and sea-ice formation processes while preserving the ecological relevance of the animal’s track ref [26].

For inference, however, coupled observation does not eliminate uncertainty; it relocates it. Environmental measurements remain constrained by tag placement, compression, transmission losses, location error, and sensor-specific biases such as conductivity offsets linked to the animal body or mounting configuration ref [25], ref [26]. Thus, biologging-derived oceanography is best treated not as a simple covariate source but as a co-observed process with its own calibration and quality-control requirements. When handled carefully, these records substantially strengthen mechanistic interpretation of putative foraging behavior and improve generalization across dynamic habitats by linking what seals do to the water masses they actually experience ref [25], ref [26].

subsections.section_title: Study Design, Ecological Context, and Generalization
subsections.subsection_title: Condition, Survival, and Broader Generalization Across Populations
subsections.content:
Inference from location and dive data is strongest when embedded in a demographic framework, because the behaviors identified as “foraging” matter ecologically only insofar as they affect condition, recruitment, and survival. In pinnipeds, body mass and condition at weaning are robust predictors of early survival in gray seals, and elevated immunoglobulin levels may further signal physiological costs or challenge not captured by movement data alone ref [85]. Mechanistically, postweaning fasting studies show that pups rely predominantly on lipid stores, but protein reserves and body composition also shape fasting endurance and likely the window available to learn to forage successfully at sea ref [8], ref [9], ref [10]. Thus, similar tracks or dive profiles can have very different fitness consequences depending on underlying state.

Long-term mark-recapture studies also show that survival is structured by age, sex, density, and environment, and that these effects vary among species and regions. Southern elephant seal survival reflects a complex interaction between intrinsic and extrinsic drivers, with environmentally mediated maternal effects sometimes overwhelming apparent density dependence ref [86]. Hawaiian monk seals exhibit strong temporal and spatial heterogeneity in age-specific survival across subpopulations, emphasizing that estimates from one colony may not represent a species-wide demographic regime ref [87]. Earlier population models for British gray seals likewise highlighted how small changes in adult survival can dominate population growth, whereas density dependence acting only through pup survival may have limited leverage ref [88].

These results caution against broad generalization from behavior-inference models trained in a single site, season, or age class. A movement state associated with area-restricted search may correspond to high prey encounter rates in one population but poor net energetic return in another if prey quality, competition, disease burden, or fasting constraints differ. Broader inference therefore requires linking behavioral classifications to independent measures of condition and survival, and testing transferability across colonies and demographic contexts rather than assuming universal relationships between inferred “foraging” behavior and fitness outcomes ref [85], ref [86], ref [87].

subsections.subsection_title: Figures and Tables
subsections.content:
Figures and tables in this survey should be designed to make uncertainty, scale, and validation explicit rather than merely illustrative. A summary figure is particularly useful for contrasting the inferential pipeline from raw locations and abstracted dive profiles to putative behavioural states, highlighting where measurement error, temporal aggregation, and model assumptions enter the analysis ref [70], ref [37], ref [35]. A complementary table can then compare common inference frameworks—threshold rules, first-passage time, state-space models, hidden Markov models, and direct prey-capture proxies—against the data resolution they require and the behavioural claims they can legitimately support ref [89], ref [59].

Because a central message of the review is that location- and dive-based proxies are not equivalent to observed feeding, at least one figure should synthesize validation studies across sensor types. A matrix or evidence map linking horizontal movement metrics, dive-shape descriptors, accelerometry, stomach temperature, and animal-borne video would clearly show where foraging inference has been validated, where it remains weakly supported, and how performance varies across species and devices ref [5], ref [11], ref [49]. This is especially important because several studies have shown that dive variables can sometimes predict foraging success, but only under specific ecological and sensor contexts ref [5], ref [6].

Tables should also standardize reporting of practical limitations that are often dispersed across methods sections, including Argos and Fastloc GPS error, tag programming choices, profile compression, and handling effects ref [37], ref [35], ref [29]. A concise checklist-style table covering sampling frequency, dive abstraction method, behavioural classification approach, validation source, and stated uncertainty would improve comparability among pinniped studies and help readers distinguish robust inference from attractive overinterpretation.
